title: A Whole Salmon, Roasted
dek: One fish, one pan, one hot oven, and the only real skill is knowing when to stop.
intro:
A whole fish looks like a project and cooks like a roast chicken with fewer opinions. The bones and the skin hold water in the meat while the oven pulls it out, so the window between right and chalky is several minutes wider than it is on a bare fillet. The trade is that you cannot see the middle, which is why a thermometer goes into the thickest part of the shoulder, alongside the backbone, and not into the belly flap.

Buy or catch a fish that fits your longest pan on the diagonal. Measure the oven before you commit to anything, because a fish that does not fit is a problem you cannot solve at the counter.

items: 1 whole salmon, 8 to 10 lb (3.6 to 4.5 kg), gutted, gills removed, scaled
1 small fennel bulb, sliced thin, optional

method: Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 400°F (205°C). Line a sheet pan with foil, then lay parchment over the foil. The foil is for the cleanup. The parchment is so the skin releases instead of welding itself to the pan.
Rinse the cavity, run a thumbnail down the backbone to clear the dark blood line, and dry the whole fish hard with paper towels. Wet skin steams. Dry skin browns.

Slash the thickest part of each side three or four times, straight down to the bone, at an angle. The cuts let heat reach the shoulder while the tail is still catching up, which is the whole problem with cooking a wedge-shaped animal evenly.
Salt the cavity and the outside, working salt into the slashes. Pack the cavity with lemon, thyme, garlic and fennel. Do not tie it shut; you want steam to move through.

Rub the outside with oil, lay the fish diagonally on the pan, and slide it in. Figure on roughly 10 minutes per inch measured at the shoulder, but treat that as a reason to start checking rather than a schedule.

Start testing early. Push the probe into the slash at the shoulder until the tip sits near the backbone. Fully cooked, by the FDA figure, is 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), at which point the flesh is opaque all the way through and separates into firm flakes under a fork.

Plenty of people pull salmon at 125 to 130 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 54°C) for a translucent middle. That is below the FDA number, and it is a real risk, not a technicality. Anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, very young or elderly should get fish taken to the full internal temperature instead.
Rest the fish on the pan for 10 minutes. It coasts upward a few degrees, and the flesh firms enough to lift cleanly. Pour the melted butter over it and scatter parsley.

To serve, run a knife along the backbone and lift the top fillet off in sections. When that side is gone, grip the tail, lift the whole spine away in one piece, and carry on. Nobody has to flip a whole salmon at the table.

What goes wrong: taking it to the point where white albumin is weeping out of every slash. That is protein squeezing water out, and it means the middle is already past. Pull earlier next time and let the rest finish the job.
notes: A fish over about 12 lb (5.4 kg) is better split into two sides and roasted flat. The shoulder on a big one will not catch up to the tail no matter how you slash it.
Save the frame. It makes better stock than any fillet trim, and there is a chowder in this collection built on it.
storage: Cooked salmon keeps in the fridge, covered, three to four days. Pick the leftovers off the bone the same night while it is easy, and the flakes go straight into cakes, chowder or a sandwich.

title: Crisp-Skin Salmon in a Pan
dek: Skin like a potato chip, and the fish underneath still translucent in the middle.
intro:
Crisp skin is not a technique so much as a water problem. Skin is wet, and wet things steam. Everything below is about removing water before the pan does, and then not moving the fish while the pan finishes the job.

The second half of the trick is that you barely cook the top. Set the fillet skin down in a hot pan, leave it alone for most of the time, and let heat climb up through the fillet. Flipping early gives you two grey faces and a soggy skin, which is what most people get and quietly accept.

items: 4 salmon fillets, skin on, about 6 oz (170 g) each, pin bones out
1 tbsp neutral oil with a high smoke point

method: Salt the skin side and set the fillets skin up on a rack over a plate. Leave them uncovered in the fridge 30 minutes, longer if you have it. The salt draws water out of the skin and the cold air takes it away. This step does more than the pan does.
Just before cooking, blot the skin again and scrape the flat of a knife across it from head end to tail. You will be surprised what comes off. Salt the flesh side now, not earlier.
Heat a heavy skillet over medium-high with the oil until it shimmers and the first wisp of smoke lifts off the surface. A pan that is not hot enough at the start is why skin sticks.
Lay the fillets in skin down, away from you, and press each one flat with a spatula for about 20 seconds. Fillets curl as the skin contracts, and a curled fillet only touches the pan in the middle.

Now leave them. Do not slide them, do not peek under. Watch the side of the fillet: opacity creeps up from the bottom like a tide line. When it has climbed roughly two thirds of the way and the skin has stopped sizzling frantically, you are close.
Drop in the butter, thyme and garlic, tilt the pan and spoon foaming butter over the top for a minute. The top face goes from raw to just set without ever touching metal.

Flip, count to 30, and take them out. Fully cooked is an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) at the thickest point, where the flesh flakes firmly and looks the same colour throughout. Cooks who prefer a translucent centre pull at 125 to 130 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 54°C), which is below the FDA figure and not for anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly or very young.
Rest skin up on a warm plate, never skin down on anything, and squeeze lemon over the flesh only. Lemon juice on the skin undoes twenty minutes of work in four seconds.
What goes wrong: crowding. Two fillets in a small pan drop the temperature, water pools, and you have poached fish with leathery skin. Cook in two batches and keep the first warm in a low oven.
notes: Nonstick works but never gets the same crackle. Carbon steel or cast iron, properly hot, is the tool for this.
Chalky salmon is salmon that went past temperature. The proteins squeeze out water and there is no getting it back. Buy a thermometer before you buy better fish.
storage: Best eaten immediately, because skin softens within minutes of resting. Leftovers keep in the fridge three days and are worth flaking cold into a salad rather than reheating.

title: Salmon on the Grill Without Losing Half of It
dek: Hot grate, clean grate, oiled grate, and the patience not to move it.
totalTime: 1 hour 30 minutes with the plank soak
intro:
Two ways to grill salmon, and the argument between them is about how much you trust your grate. Straight on the bars gives you smoke, char and grill marks, and it will tear a fillet apart if the grate is dirty or the fish is moved too soon. A soaked cedar plank gives up the char and gains a guarantee, because the fish never touches metal at all.

Both are here. Pick by how much you care about the fish surviving intact in front of company, which is a legitimate way to make a cooking decision.

items: 1 salmon side, about 2.5 lb (1.1 kg), skin on, pin bones out

method: If you are planking, submerge the cedar in cold water for at least an hour, weighted down with a can. A dry plank is kindling, and you will find that out at the worst moment.

Mix salt, brown sugar and paprika and rub it over the flesh side. Let the side sit at room temperature 20 minutes while the grill comes up. The sugar helps colour; the salt firms the surface so it is less inclined to shred.
Build a two-zone fire: coals banked on one side, nothing on the other, or half the burners lit. You want the hot side around 450°F (230°C) with the lid down and a genuinely cool side to retreat to.

Scrape the grate clean while it is hot, then wipe it with a folded towel dipped in oil, held in tongs. Repeat twice. A clean, hot, oiled grate is the entire difference between grilled salmon and salmon scraped off with a putty knife.

Straight on the grate: oil the fish, lay it skin down over the hot side, and close the lid. Do not touch it. The skin will release on its own when it has set, which takes several minutes. If it resists a gentle lift with a thin spatula, it is not ready.

Slide the fillet to the cool side once the skin has crisped and darkened, then close the lid and let it coast. Brush with the honey glaze in the last few minutes only, because honey over direct heat turns to carbon quickly.

On a plank: lay lemon slices on the wet plank, fish on top, plank over the hot side until the edges of the board smoke and darken, then move the whole thing to the cool side and close the lid. Keep a spray bottle handy in case a corner catches.

Either way, go by the probe. Fully cooked is an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), with the flesh opaque and flaking cleanly. If you prefer a rosy middle, cooks commonly pull at 125 to 130 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 54°C), which is below the FDA figure and should be skipped by anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly or very young.
Slide two spatulas under the fillet to move it, or leave the skin behind on purpose and lift the flesh off in pieces. Both are respectable. Rest 5 minutes before serving.
What goes wrong: flipping. A side of salmon does not need turning over. Skin down the whole way, lid closed, is the method with the fewest ways to fail.
notes: Planks are single use if they char through, and good for a second run if they only scorch. They are not worth cleaning and re-soaking more than once.
Skin-off fillets on a grate are for people who enjoy suffering. Buy skin on.
storage: Fridge, covered, three to four days. Cold grilled salmon on toast with something sharp is arguably better than the first serving.

title: Poached Salmon in Court Bouillon
dek: The gentlest way to cook a fish, and the one that punishes a rolling boil hardest.
intro:
Poaching has a bad reputation because most people boil the fish and call it poaching. Water at a genuine boil hammers the outside of a fillet into cotton before the middle registers anything. Water held just below a simmer, where a bubble surfaces every few seconds and nothing else moves, cooks salmon into something silky that no pan can match.

Court bouillon is the flavoured liquid it happens in: water, wine, acid, aromatics, salt, simmered briefly first so the fish takes on something instead of leaching into plain water. It is worth the fifteen minutes.

items: 6 salmon portions, about 6 oz (170 g) each, skin on or off

method: Put every court bouillon ingredient in a wide pan deep enough to cover the fish by an inch. Bring it up, then hold it at a lazy simmer 20 minutes so the vegetables give up something. Strain if you want a clean look, or leave it rustic.

Let the liquid drop until it stops bubbling. You want it hovering somewhere around 175°F (80°C), which looks like steam rising and one bubble every few seconds. If you have a thermometer, use it; if not, water at this stage is silent.
Lower the portions in, skin down, in one layer. They should be covered. Add hot water if they are not, and accept the slight dilution.

Hold the heat there, uncovered, adjusting the burner constantly if it is a gas ring that likes to surge. Nothing should roll. Small fillets take under 10 minutes and thick centre cuts a little longer, so start checking early.

Test with a probe in the thickest part. Fully cooked is an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C); the fish looks matte, gives no resistance to a fork, and separates into large soft flakes. The lower pull of 125 to 130 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 54°C) is popular but below the FDA figure, and not appropriate for anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly or very young.
Lift the portions out with a slotted spatula and drain on a towel. If you are serving them cold, let them cool in the liquid off the heat instead, which keeps them from tightening up.
Stir the creme fraiche with dill, lemon and horseradish, and season it. Serve alongside, warm or cold.

What goes wrong: a boil. A boil moves fish around, tears the flakes apart at the seams and pushes white albumin out in ugly curds. The moment you see the surface churn, pull the pan halfway off the burner.
notes: The strained bouillon can be reduced hard and used as the base of a sauce, or frozen for a chowder. Do not throw it out.
This is the method for a whole cold side on a platter. Poach, cool in the liquid overnight, then peel the skin off and scrape the grey line away before it goes on the table.
storage: Poached salmon keeps three days in the fridge, better if it sits in a little of its own liquid so it does not dry at the edges.

title: Cold Smoke and Hot Smoke, Explained
dek: Two entirely different processes that share a word, and only one of them cooks anything.
yield: One clear head about which one you want
activeTime: 30 minutes of reading and setting up
totalTime: Varies by method, from half a day to three days
intro:
People use the word smoked to mean two processes that have almost nothing in common. Hot smoking cooks the fish in smoke, somewhere above 150°F (66°C), and produces flaky, opaque, fully cooked fish that keeps in a fridge for about a week. Cold smoking flavours fish with smoke at a temperature deliberately too low to cook it, which means the salt cure is doing all the preservation work and the smoke is doing none of it.

This piece is the explanation, not a recipe. Read it before you build anything, because the failure mode of the second one is not a bad dinner.

items: 1 smoker capable of holding 175 to 225°F (80 to 107°C)
1 smoke generator separated from the fish chamber
1 way to keep the chamber under about 80 degrees Fahrenheit (27°C)
1 tested cure recipe you did not invent
1 thermometer for the chamber, not the fish

method: Understand what smoke does. Smoke deposits phenols and acids on the surface of the fish. Those slow surface spoilage and taste good. They do not sterilise anything and they do not reach the middle of a fillet in any meaningful quantity.

Hot smoking is cooking. You hold a chamber at 175 to 225°F (80 to 107°C) and take the fish to an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), at which point it is opaque, firm, and flakes apart under a fork. It is a cooked food and it is handled like one.

Cold smoking is not cooking. The chamber is kept cool enough that the fish never sets, which puts the whole product in the temperature range bacteria like most, for hours. The only thing standing between you and a problem is a salt cure of the right strength, held for the right time, at refrigeration temperature.

Because of that, do not improvise a cold smoke. Use a tested cure with a stated salt concentration and a stated time, and follow it exactly. The bacterium people worry about here is Clostridium botulinum, which is happy without oxygen, and it does not announce itself by taste or smell.

Know what freezing does and does not do. Freezing at commercial parameters is used to address parasites in fish intended to be eaten raw or lightly cured. It does not kill bacteria, and it does not make an unsafe cure safe. If you want the current guidance, read what the FDA publishes on parasite destruction rather than taking anybody's word for it, including ours.

Pick by what you actually want. If you want flaky, warm, smoky fish for a chowder or a sandwich, you want hot smoke, and it is forgiving. If you want silky translucent slices for a bagel, you want a cold smoke or a cure like gravlax, and it is not.

Build the right equipment for the job. Hot smoking needs a firebox, a chamber and a probe. Cold smoking needs the smoke source physically separated from the fish, usually a tube or a pellet generator feeding a cool box, and it works badly on a warm day for reasons that should now be obvious.

Decide who is eating it. Cold-smoked fish is a ready-to-eat product that gets no further heat step, and public health guidance has long steered pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly and very young people away from it. Hot-smoked fish taken to temperature carries no such caveat.
notes: Local smokehouses exist for exactly this reason. The half pound of smoked salmon in our cooler was made by people with a licensed process and a temperature log.
If a recipe you find online for cold smoke does not state a salt percentage and a cure time, it is not a recipe. It is a photograph with words under it.
storage: Hot-smoked fish: fridge about a week, freezer three months. Cold-smoked fish: follow the cure's own guidance, keep it cold, and treat it as a short-life product, not a shelf-stable one.

title: Hot-Smoked Salmon
dek: A brine you can measure, a chamber you can hold, and a number you stop at.
totalTime: About 18 hours including brine and drying
intro:
Hot smoking is a cooking method with a brine in front of it, and both halves matter. The brine seasons through the fillet, firms the proteins so the fish does not fall apart, and sets up the pellicle that smoke sticks to. The smoke chamber then cooks it slowly enough that the outside does not seize before the middle arrives.

The measurements below are given as a percentage of the weight of water, because scaling a brine by cups of salt across different salt crystal sizes is how people end up with fish that is either bland or inedible. Weigh it.

items: 120 g fine sea salt, which is 6 percent of the water weight
2.5 lb (1.1 kg) salmon fillet, skin on, cut into portions of even thickness
1 tbsp neutral oil for the rack

method: Dissolve the salt and sugar completely in a litre of the water, whisking until the liquid runs clear rather than cloudy, then add the rest of the water cold along with the pepper and bay. Undissolved salt at the bottom of a bucket is salt that is not in your fish.

Submerge the fish, weighted down with a plate, and refrigerate. Thin belly pieces need about 4 hours; portions an inch thick want 8 to 12. Over-brining is real, and it shows up as fish too salty to eat with anything.
Rinse the fillets under cold water, pat dry, and set them skin down on an oiled rack. Refrigerate uncovered 4 to 12 hours, or sit them in front of a fan in a cool room for 2 to 3 hours.

Wait for the pellicle. The surface should go from wet to dull and slightly tacky, like the back of an envelope. Smoke does not adhere to a wet fillet; it beads up and runs off, and you get pale fish that tastes of nothing much.
Bring the smoker to 175°F (80°C) with alder going. Load the fish, leaving room around each piece for air to move, and close it up.

Hold the chamber between 175 and 225°F (80 and 107°C). Lower and slower is better for texture, hotter is faster and drier. Expect two to four hours depending on thickness and how well your box holds heat on a wet coastal afternoon.

Cook to an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) at the thickest point. At that number the flesh is opaque through, firm to a fingertip, and flakes into clean sheets. Do not run a hot smoke to a lower temperature; the whole point of hot smoke is that it is a cooked product.

Watch for white albumin beading along the surface. A little is normal. A lot means the chamber is running hot and the fish is squeezing out water, and the finished fillet will be dry no matter what you do next.
Cool the fish on the rack at room temperature for half an hour, then refrigerate uncovered until cold before wrapping. Wrapping warm fish traps steam and softens everything you just built.
notes: Alder is the local wood and the traditional one for salmon here. Fruit woods are gentler, hickory and mesquite will bury the fish.
A 6 percent brine is a middle setting. Drop to 4 percent for a mild result you can eat in slabs, go to 8 percent for something closer to a preserved product that you use in small amounts.
storage: Fridge, wrapped, about a week. Vacuum sealed and frozen, three months without much loss. It thaws well, which is more than can be said for most cooked fish.

title: Salmon Cakes That Hold Together
dek: The binder is the whole argument, and most recipes get the ratio wrong in favour of bread.
intro:
A salmon cake is a way of turning the far end of a fillet, or last night's leftovers, into something people are pleased to see. The failure is always the same: too much filler and it eats like stuffing, too little and it collapses in the pan into an expensive hash.

The fix is not more breadcrumbs. It is a small amount of binder, a proper chill so the fat sets, and gentle handling that keeps recognisable flakes intact instead of mashing everything into paste. You want to see the fish in the finished cake.

items: 1 lb (450 g) cooked salmon, flaked, skin and bones removed

method: If you are starting from raw fish, cook it first: bake portions at 350°F (175°C) until they flake apart easily and reach an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), then cool completely. Warm fish will not bind.

Flake the salmon into a bowl in pieces roughly the size of a thumbnail. Do not shred it. Pull out any pin bones and the grey layer under the skin, which is oily and strong and does the finished cake no favours.

Whisk egg, mayonnaise, mustard and lemon juice together separately, then fold that into the fish with the shallot, herbs, salt, pepper and three quarters cup of panko. Fold, do not stir. Twelve strokes, not forty.
Squeeze a small handful. It should just hold. If it slumps, add panko a tablespoon at a time; if it feels dry and crumbly, another spoon of mayonnaise. This is the only judgement call in the recipe.

Shape eight cakes about three quarters of an inch thick, set them on a lined tray, and refrigerate at least an hour. The chill is not optional. It sets the fat and the egg, and it is the difference between a cake and a scramble.
Press both faces into the remaining panko. Heat oil and butter in a heavy skillet over medium until the butter foam subsides and a crumb dropped in sizzles steadily rather than violently.

Fry in batches, without crowding, until the underside is deep golden and a spatula slides under cleanly, then flip once. They are hot through when the centre steams as you press the side and a probe reads 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C).
Drain on a rack, not on paper. Paper traps steam and softens the crust you just spent ten minutes building.
Stir the sauce ingredients together and serve alongside with lemon.
What goes wrong: flipping too early. If you have to force a spatula under, the crust has not formed and it will tear. Wait for it to release.
notes: Canned or hot-smoked salmon both work. Smoked is stronger; cut it with an equal weight of plain cooked fish or the whole plate tastes like a campfire.
The cakes freeze well raw. Freeze on the tray, bag them, and fry from frozen over lower heat with a lid on for the first few minutes.
storage: Shaped raw cakes hold two days in the fridge. Cooked cakes keep three days and reheat best in a hot oven on a rack, never in a microwave.

title: A Salmon Chowder Base
dek: Build the base right and the fish goes in last, for four minutes, off the boil.
intro:
Most bad chowder is bad because the fish was in the pot the entire time. Salmon goes from silky to woolly in about ninety seconds of hard simmering, and once it has gone there is no route back. So the base is built and seasoned as a complete thing on its own, and the fish is stirred in at the end and barely cooked by residual heat.

This makes about three quarts of base. It freezes, which means a pot on a Sunday turns into four fast dinners on wet weeknights when nobody wants to think.

items: 1 leek, white and pale green, sliced and washed
2 lb (900 g) waxy potatoes, in 3/4 inch dice
1 tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste
1.5 lb (680 g) salmon, skin off, in 1 inch cubes

method: Render the bacon in a heavy pot over medium heat until the fat has run out and the pieces are browned at the edges but not brittle. Lift the bacon out and set it aside; leave the fat.
Add the butter, then onion, celery and leek. Cook until everything has slumped and gone translucent and the onion smells sweet rather than sharp, with no colour on it.

Stir in the garlic for a minute, then the flour. Keep it moving until the raw flour smell is gone and the vegetables are coated in a pale paste. Undercooked flour tastes exactly like undercooked flour and it will follow you all the way to the bowl.
Pour in the stock a cup at a time, whisking each addition smooth before the next. Add potatoes, bay, thyme, salt and pepper.

Bring it to a bare simmer and hold it there until the potatoes give way completely to a knife tip with no resistance in the middle, roughly 20 minutes depending on the variety. Fish out the bay leaves.
Crush a few potatoes against the side of the pot with a spoon. That starch is your thickener, and it beats adding more flour.
Stop here if you are freezing it. Cool the base fast, in a shallow pan, and freeze in quart portions. Cream and fish go in at serving time, never before.
To finish a pot: bring the base back to a gentle simmer, stir in the cream and corn and let it come back up to steaming. Then take the pot off the heat entirely.

Slide the salmon cubes in, stir once, and put the lid on. They cook in the residual heat in about 4 minutes, until they turn opaque and break apart at a nudge from a spoon, reaching an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C). If your pieces are large, check one with a probe.
Add dill, lemon juice and the reserved bacon. Taste for salt now and not before, because the bacon and stock have both been quietly seasoning it.
notes: Hot-smoked salmon instead of raw makes a different and very good soup. Use half the weight and add it with the dill, since it is already cooked.
Waxy potatoes hold their shape. Russets disintegrate into the broth, which some people want and most do not.
storage: Finished chowder keeps two days in the fridge and does not freeze well once the fish is in. Plain base freezes three months.

title: Gravlax, Cured Not Cooked
dek: Salt, sugar, dill, weight and three days of doing nothing.
yield: One cured side, about 2 lb (900 g)
intro:
Gravlax is a salt and sugar cure that draws water out of a salmon fillet and firms it into something you can slice thin enough to read through. There is no heat at any point. The fish never reaches a cooked internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), and it is not supposed to; the salt is doing the work that the oven usually does.

Which means the safety thinking is different. This is a raw ready-to-eat product. Start with fish you trust from a source you trust, keep it cold the whole way through, and read the note at the bottom before you decide who at the table is eating it.

items: 1 salmon fillet, skin on, about 2 lb (900 g), centre cut, pin bones out
2 large bunches dill, stems and all, roughly chopped

method: Run your fingers along the fillet against the grain and pull every pin bone with pliers. Slicing thin later is miserable if you are working around bones you meant to remove and did not.
Mix salt, sugar, pepper and coriander. Note the ratio is equal weights of salt and sugar, which is the classic setting; more salt firms it faster and makes it saltier, more sugar softens both.

Lay a long sheet of plastic wrap in a dish. Spread a third of the cure on it, then a third of the dill, then the fillet skin down. Sprinkle the spirit over the flesh if you are using it, then pack the rest of the cure and dill over the top, thicker at the thick end.

Wrap tightly, set the dish in the fridge, and put something heavy on top: a board with two cans on it, or a foil-wrapped brick. The weight presses liquid out and keeps the cure in contact with the flesh.
Turn the parcel once a day. Liquid will pool in the dish; that is water leaving the fish and it means the cure is working. Do not pour it back.

After three days the fillet should feel firm all the way to the middle when pressed with a finger, with no soft give at the thick end, and the colour should have gone deeper and more translucent. Thin fillets can be ready in two days, a thick king side may want four.
Unwrap, scrape the cure off, and rinse briefly under cold water only if it tastes too salty at the edge. Pat dry and refrigerate uncovered an hour to firm the surface for slicing.
Slice on a long shallow angle, almost parallel to the board, starting at the tail. Stop at the skin. A thin flexible knife and slow hands beat a sharp knife and hurry.
For the sauce, whisk both mustards with sugar and vinegar, then dribble the oil in while whisking until it thickens like a loose mayonnaise, and stir in the dill.

Safety, plainly: this is raw cured fish. Anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly or very young should not eat it. If you want the current guidance on freezing fish intended to be eaten raw or lightly cured, read what the FDA publishes on the subject rather than relying on any recipe, this one included. Freezing addresses parasites; it does nothing about bacteria.
notes: Skin on, always. It gives you something to slice against and it holds the fillet together under weight.
The cure is not reusable. Throw it out.
storage: Wrapped tight in the fridge, about a week. Slices dry out fast, so cut only what you are putting on the plate. It freezes for a month but the texture goes slightly grainy on thawing.

title: Canning Salmon, Pressure Canner Only
dek: Fish is a low-acid food, and a boiling water bath cannot make it safe. Not ever.
yield: Depends on your canner and jar size
intro:
Home canned salmon is one of the genuinely great things you can do with a heavy season. It is also the single most dangerous recipe in this collection, so this page tells you how to pack the jars and then sends you somewhere else for the numbers, on purpose.

Fish is low acid. Water at a rolling boil tops out at 212 degrees Fahrenheit (100°C) at sea level and that is nowhere near hot enough to destroy Clostridium botulinum spores. Only a pressure canner, holding roughly 240°F (116°C) under pressure, does that. There is no workaround, no amount of lemon juice, and no old family method that changes this.

items: 10 lb (4.5 kg) fresh salmon, gutted, bled, chilled since it came out of the water
1 tsp canning salt per pint jar, optional and for flavour only
1 dial or weighted gauge pressure canner, tested for accuracy
12 half-pint or pint jars with new lids and sound rings
1 jar lifter, 1 wide funnel, 1 bubble tool
1 copy of the current USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or your OSU Extension office on the phone

method: Before anything else, get the tested figures. Look up the current process for fish in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or call your county Extension office, which in this state is OSU Extension. Processing time and pressure change with jar size and with your altitude, and this page is deliberately not printing a number for you to misapply.

Altitude matters more than people expect. Siletz sits close to sea level, so the sea level figures apply here. If you are canning at elevation anywhere inland, your pressure has to go up, and the tested tables tell you by how much. Look up your own altitude and use the line that matches it.

Start with fish that has been handled properly. Bled at the water, gutted quickly, on ice since. Canning does not rescue fish that sat warm in a tote all afternoon; it seals in whatever was already happening.

Rinse the fillets, remove the fins and the tail, and cut crosswise into lengths that stand upright in your jars. Leave the skin and the bones in. Both soften completely under pressure and the bones are where a lot of the calcium is.

Pack the pieces in vertically, skin against the glass, filling firmly without crushing. Fish gives up plenty of its own liquid, so add no water. Leave the headspace your tested recipe specifies, which for fish is generally more than you would guess.

Add salt if you want it, run the bubble tool around the inside, wipe every rim with a clean damp cloth until it squeaks, and fit lids and rings finger tight. A speck of fish oil on a rim is a seal that fails in the cupboard three weeks later.

Load the canner with the water your manufacturer specifies, lock it down, and vent steam in a steady column for the full ten minutes before you close the vent. Skipping the vent traps air, and trapped air means the inside of that canner is cooler than the gauge claims.

Bring it to the pressure your tested recipe gives and start timing only when it is there and holding. Adjust the burner constantly to keep it steady. If the pressure drops below target at any point, you bring it back up and start the timing over from the beginning. That is the rule and it is not negotiable.

When time is up, kill the heat and let the canner depressurise on its own. Do not run it under water, do not lift the weight to hurry it. Then wait the extra ten minutes, remove the lid away from your face, and lift jars straight up onto a towel.

Leave them alone overnight. Check every seal the next day by pressing the centre of the lid; a sealed lid does not move or click. Anything unsealed goes in the fridge and gets eaten within a couple of days, not re-processed.

Never taste-test a suspect jar. If a lid is bulging, if the contents spurt on opening, if it smells wrong, or if you have any doubt about whether the process was followed, dispose of it without tasting and follow the disposal instructions in the USDA guide. Botulinum toxin gives you no warning you can detect.
notes: A dial gauge canner should be tested for accuracy once a season. Extension offices do this, often free. A gauge reading two pounds light is a whole batch of unsafe jars.
Half-pints are the useful size. A pint of canned salmon is more than most households get through before it wants using up.
storage: Rings off, jars wiped, labelled without a date on the glass if you like, but write something on the lid so you know which batch is which. Cool dark cupboard, best quality within a year. Once open, fridge, and use in three or four days.

title: Whole Baked Steelhead with Brown Butter
dek: Leaner than salmon, less forgiving, and better than either when it is caught right.
intro:
Steelhead is a rainbow trout that went to sea and came back with opinions. It looks like salmon, it prices like a bargain, and it cooks faster because it carries less fat. That last part is the whole story: the buffer that lets a fatty king coast through an extra four minutes is not there, so a steelhead side goes from perfect to dry while you are washing a bowl.

So this is a moderate oven, a probe left in, and a brown butter poured over at the end to put back some of the richness the fish does not have on its own.

items: 1 steelhead side, about 2.5 lb (1.1 kg), skin on, pin bones out

method: Take the fish out of the fridge 20 minutes before it goes in. A side straight from cold cooks unevenly, thin end first, and steelhead has no margin for that.
Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Lower than you would use for salmon, because the goal is to narrow the gap between the surface and the middle.
Dry the fillet, salt and pepper it, rub with oil, and lay it skin down on a parchment-lined sheet pan. Tuck the thin tail end under itself so the whole side is roughly one thickness.

Bake until a probe in the thickest part reads an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) and the flesh is opaque, firming under a fingertip, and just beginning to separate along the muscle lines. In a moderate oven this is roughly 20 to 25 minutes for a side of this size, but the probe decides, not the clock.

If you like a translucent centre, cooks routinely pull at 125 to 130 degrees Fahrenheit (52 to 54°C). That is below the FDA figure and it is not the right call for anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly or very young.

While it bakes, melt the butter in a small pale-coloured pan over medium heat. Let it foam, then keep going, swirling, until the foam falls, the milk solids on the bottom turn the colour of a hazelnut shell and the whole kitchen smells like toffee. That happens fast and it burns two seconds later.
Pull the pan off the heat immediately and add the capers, which will spit, then the lemon juice, parsley and chile.
Rest the fish 5 minutes, pour the brown butter over the whole side, and serve straight off the pan.
What goes wrong: treating steelhead like a king salmon. Same shape, half the fat, two thirds the cooking time. If your last one was dry, the fish was not the problem.
notes: Hatchery steelhead and wild steelhead cook the same. What you may keep and where is an Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife question and the regulations move, so check with ODFW rather than a recipe page.
The same treatment works for a large lake trout or a big rainbow, at the same temperature, checked earlier.
storage: Fridge three days. Cold steelhead flakes into a salad better than it reheats, and reheating is what dries it out the rest of the way.

title: Trout in a Pan, Whole
dek: Cornmeal, bacon fat, a hot skillet, and a fish that fits it.
intro:
A pan-sized trout is a nearly perfect object. It cooks in under ten minutes, it needs almost nothing done to it, and the bones lift out in one piece if you cook it whole rather than filleting a fish that barely has a fillet on it.

The dusting matters. Cornmeal or a cornmeal and flour mix gives a sandy crust that browns hard and stays crisp, where plain flour goes gummy against the wet skin. Bacon fat is traditional in this part of the world for the obvious reason that there was usually some in the pan already.

items: 2 whole trout, 10 to 12 oz (280 to 340 g) each, gutted, gills out, heads on or off
3 tbsp bacon fat, or 2 tbsp neutral oil and 1 tbsp butter

method: Rinse the cavities and scrape out the dark line along the spine with a thumbnail. Dry the fish inside and out, thoroughly, then salt and pepper them inside and out.
Slash each side twice on the diagonal, no deeper than a quarter inch. This stops the skin contracting and curling the fish off the pan.
Tuck thyme, lemon slices and garlic into the cavities. Mix cornmeal, flour and paprika on a plate and press each fish into it on both sides, then shake off everything that is not clinging.

Heat the fat in a heavy skillet over medium-high until a pinch of cornmeal dropped in sizzles at once and starts to colour within a few seconds. Too cool and the coating absorbs fat instead of frying in it.

Lay the fish in, away from you, and leave them. Fry until the underside is deep golden brown and the crust releases when you nudge it, roughly 4 minutes for a fish this size, longer for anything thicker.

Flip once, with a fish slice and your other hand, and cook the second side. The fish is done when the flesh at the thickest point behind the head is opaque to the bone, the dorsal fin pulls out with no resistance, and a probe reads an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C).
Squeeze lemon into the pan, let it hiss, and spoon the pan fat over the fish once before lifting them out.
To eat: run a knife down the backbone, fold the top fillet open, then lift the whole skeleton from the tail. What is left underneath is boneless.
What goes wrong: a fish too big for the pan, curled into an arc so only the middle touches. Buy or keep trout that fit the skillet flat, or cut the head off to buy yourself two inches.
notes: Bacon first, then trout in the fat, then the bacon crumbled over at the end, is the version most people here grew up on.
If the skin sticks every time, your pan was not hot enough or you moved the fish too soon. It is almost never the fish.
storage: Eat it now. Fried whole trout does not keep well and reheating turns the crust to paste. Any leftover flesh is fine cold, picked off the bone within a day.

title: Fish and Chips
dek: Two fryings for the chips, one for the fish, and a batter mixed at the last possible second.
intro:
The chips are the harder half and nobody admits it. Potatoes have to be cooked through at a low temperature and then blistered at a high one, with a rest in between, or you get grease-logged sticks that were raw in the middle ten seconds before they burned. The fish is comparatively easy: dry it, dust it, batter it, fry it once.

Everything here depends on oil temperature holding steady, which means a thermometer and small batches. A pot of oil that drops when the food goes in is the reason home frying gets a bad name.

items: 2.5 lb (1.1 kg) russet potatoes, cut in 1/2 inch batons
2 tbsp white vinegar for the soaking water
2 tsp fine sea salt for finishing
4 pieces rockfish, lingcod or true cod, 6 oz (170 g) each, skin off
1.5 cups beer, very cold, or cold sparkling water
8 cups neutral frying oil, or enough for 3 inches in the pot
1 malt vinegar bottle for the table

method: Soak the cut potatoes in cold water with the vinegar for 30 minutes, then drain and dry them completely on towels. The soak rinses off surface starch; the drying keeps the oil from erupting.

Heat the oil to 325°F (165°C). Blanch the chips in batches until they are floppy, pale and cooked through, giving no resistance when you press one against the side of the pot. They should take on no colour at all at this stage.
Lift them onto a rack and let them cool at least 20 minutes. This rest lets moisture migrate outward and is why the second fry crisps instead of steaming. You can hold them here for hours.

Bring the oil up to 375°F (190°C). Dry the fish hard, salt it, and dust it in the plain flour, shaking off the excess. Batter will not stick to a wet fillet and will slide off in the pot in one sad sheet.

Now mix the batter, and not before. Whisk the dry ingredients, pour in the cold beer, and stir just until it comes together with lumps still visible. The consistency should coat a spoon like thin pancake batter. Overmixing builds gluten and gluten makes armour, not crust.
Dip one fillet, let the excess run off for a second, and lower it into the oil tail first, holding for a moment before you let go so it sets rather than sinking to the bottom.

Fry two pieces at a time until the batter is deep golden and rigid, the bubbling has slowed noticeably, and the fish inside reaches an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) with flesh that flakes cleanly. Expect five or six minutes for a thick piece.

Rest the fish on a rack in a low oven while you finish the chips. Return the chips to the 375°F (190°C) oil in batches until they are blistered, deep gold and audibly hard when they knock against the spider.
Salt the chips the instant they come out, while the surface is still greasy enough to hold it. Salt applied a minute later just falls off.
What goes wrong: crowding the pot. Every piece you add drops the oil temperature, and oil below about 325°F (165°C) soaks in instead of sealing. Fry less at a time than feels efficient.
notes: Rockfish, lingcod and true cod all work. Halibut is a waste of money in batter and dries out faster than any of them.
Beer contributes carbon dioxide and a little alcohol, which flashes off fast and helps drying. Cold sparkling water does most of the same job if you would rather not use beer.
storage: Neither half keeps. Fried fish is a thing you eat standing up. Strain and save the oil once it has cooled, and it is good for several more rounds of fish before it starts smelling like the last thing you cooked.

title: A Fry Batter That Stays Crisp
dek: Why the first bite is always good and the fifth one usually is not.
yield: Enough for about 2 lb (900 g) of fish
intro:
Batter goes soft for one reason: steam. Water inside the fish turns to vapour, the vapour has to get out through the crust, and a dense crust traps it until the whole shell turns to wallpaper paste. Everything a good batter does is aimed at building a shell that is rigid, dry and porous enough to let that steam leave.

Three levers do most of the work. Cut the gluten with a starch that cannot form any. Keep the batter cold so it does not develop while it waits. Get carbon dioxide into it so the coating fries with holes in it. This page is the batter and the reasoning, ready for any fish you like.

items: 1.5 cups sparkling water or lager, refrigerator cold
2 tbsp vodka, optional, and it does help
1/2 cup rice flour for the dredge

method: Understand the dredge first. A thin coat of plain rice flour on dry fish gives the batter something to grip. Skip it and the batter slides off in the oil, every time, and you spend the evening fishing shreds out with a spider.

Whisk the dry ingredients together and chill the bowl. Chill the liquid too. Cold slows gluten development, and it widens the gap between batter temperature and oil temperature, which means the shell sets faster on contact.
Heat the oil to 375°F (190°C) before you mix anything wet. The batter should wait for the oil, not the other way round.
Pour the cold liquid into the dry and stir with chopsticks or a fork until it is just combined and still lumpy. Lumps are fine. Smooth batter is overworked batter, and it fries into a chewy skin.
Check the consistency by lifting the fork. It should fall in a ribbon that sinks back in about two seconds. Too thick and it fries into bread; too thin and it fries into lace.

Dredge the dry fish in rice flour, shake it off, dip, and lower it into the oil. Fry until the coating is rigid, pale gold rather than dark, and the bubbling around the piece has dropped from a furious boil to a lazy simmer. That change in sound is the water leaving; when it slows, the inside is cooked.

Confirm with a probe. Fish is done at an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), opaque and flaking. Batter hides everything, so check the first piece of every batch until you know your timings.
Drain on a rack over a tray, never on paper towel, and never stacked. Steam trapped under a piece of fish will undo the crust in under a minute.
If you are holding a batch, keep it on the rack in an oven at 200°F (95°C) with the door cracked. That keeps drying the shell instead of steaming it.
What goes wrong, in order of likelihood: wet fish, warm batter, cold oil, crowded pot, paper towel. Fix them in that order.
notes: The vodka works because alcohol evaporates faster than water and inhibits gluten. Two tablespoons is enough to notice; more thins the batter without helping further.
For a gluten-free version, use all rice flour and cornstarch in place of the wheat flour. It is arguably crisper and slightly more fragile.
storage: Mix the dry blend in quantity and keep it in a jar in the cupboard for months. Mixed batter is good for about twenty minutes and then it is a different, worse batter.

title: Rockfish Tacos
dek: The cheapest good fish on this coast, in a hot pan, with cabbage and lime.
intro:
Rockfish is what people bring back from a bottom fishing trip out of Depoe Bay when the tuna did not happen and the halibut season was not open. It is firm, mild, white, cheap, and it holds together in a pan better than cod does, which makes it the right fish for a taco.

These are pan-seared rather than fried, mostly because a taco already has enough going on and partly because nobody wants to heat eight cups of oil on a Tuesday. The slaw is doing the work that a batter would otherwise do: crunch, acid, and something cold against something hot.

items: 1.5 lb (680 g) rockfish fillets, skin off, cut in 1 inch strips

method: Toss the cabbage and onion with lime juice, honey and salt and let it sit while you do everything else. Twenty minutes in acid takes the raw edge off the onion and wilts the cabbage just enough to fold into a tortilla.
Stir the crema ingredients together and taste for heat. One chipotle is mild in this quantity; two is not.
Mix the spices with the salt and toss the fish strips in it, coating all sides. Do this right before cooking, because salt sitting on cut fish draws water and you will be searing wet fish.
Warm the tortillas first, directly over a gas flame or dry in a hot skillet, until they puff slightly and take a few dark spots. Stack them in a folded towel to steam soft.
Heat the oil in a heavy skillet over medium-high until it shimmers. Lay the strips in one layer with space between them and do not touch them.

Sear until the underside has a real brown crust and the strips release from the pan on their own, then turn each one. Rockfish is done when it is opaque to the centre, flakes at a fork, and reaches an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C). In strips this size that is a couple of minutes a side.
Squeeze lime over the fish in the pan off the heat, and break the strips into rough chunks with a spatula.
Build: tortilla, crema, fish, drained slaw, avocado, more lime. Drain the slaw or the tortilla goes to pieces before it reaches your mouth.
What goes wrong: overcooking, which turns rockfish stringy and dry rather than chalky the way salmon goes. Pull it a shade early and let the residual heat finish it in the pan off the burner.
notes: Lingcod, true cod, sablefish and halibut trim all work here. So does the awkward tail end of a salmon fillet if that is what is in the fridge.
Doubling the spice mix and keeping it in a jar makes this a fifteen minute dinner the second time.
storage: The slaw and crema keep three days. Cooked fish keeps two, and is better folded into a cold taco than reheated into a hot one.

title: Seared Halibut, Butter Basted
dek: Expensive, lean, and unforgiving. Cook it like a steak and stop early.
intro:
Halibut costs what it costs, and the whole risk of the evening sits in a window of about ninety seconds. It has almost no fat, which means nothing is protecting the muscle fibres once they start to tighten. Overcooked halibut is not merely dry, it is cottony and slightly squeaky, and it happened while you were plating the vegetables.

Treat a thick halibut steak or a centre-cut fillet like a small beef steak: dry surface, hot pan, hard sear on one side only, then butter and a spoon and low heat to bring the middle up gently. Have the probe in your hand before the fish goes in.

items: 4 halibut portions, 6 to 7 oz (170 to 200 g) each, at least 1 inch thick
2 tbsp grapeseed or other high smoke point oil

method: Take the fish out of the fridge 20 minutes ahead and salt it on all sides. Set it on a rack, uncovered, so the surface dries. A dry surface browns; a wet one grey-steams and never gets a crust.
Heat a heavy skillet over medium-high with the oil until it is shimmering and just about to smoke. Halibut needs a genuinely hot pan for the first thirty seconds and a much cooler one afterwards.
Lay the portions in, presentation side down, and press each briefly with a spatula so the whole face makes contact. Then leave them entirely alone.

Sear until the edge you can see has gone opaque about a third of the way up and the underside is a deep even gold that releases from the pan without tearing. Peeking early is how the crust gets left behind in the pan.

Turn the heat down to medium-low, flip the fish, and add butter, thyme, garlic and lemon peel. As the butter foams, tilt the pan and spoon it over the fish continuously. This is a gentle finish, not a second sear.

Probe the thickest portion. Fully cooked halibut is an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), where it is opaque throughout and the flakes separate in large sheets. Many cooks pull halibut a few degrees short and let it carry over on the plate; if you go lower than the FDA figure, understand that is a choice with a risk attached, and not one for anyone pregnant, immunocompromised, elderly or very young.
Rest on a warm plate 3 minutes. Halibut carries over more than you expect because of its density, so the pan is not the last place it cooks.
Add lemon juice to the pan butter off the heat, swirl, and pour it over. Finish with chives and flaky salt.

What goes wrong: thin portions. Anything under an inch will be past temperature before it browns. If your fillet is thin, skip the sear entirely and bake it at 300°F (150°C) until it is just opaque instead.
notes: Cheeks are the best part of the fish and the cheapest, and they cook in about two minutes. Treat them like scallops.
Halibut seasons and limits are managed and change from year to year. That is a Fish and Wildlife question, not a kitchen one.
storage: Fridge, two days, and be honest that it is a shadow of the first serving. Leftover halibut is better repurposed cold into a salad or warmed gently into a chowder than reheated on a plate.

title: A Whole Fish Baked on a Bed of Potatoes
dek: The potatoes cook in the drippings, which is the entire reason to do it this way.
intro:
People are shy about whole fish because of the head, which is silly, because a whole fish is easier to cook well than a fillet and costs less per pound of edible meat. Bones conduct heat inward and the skin keeps water in, so the margin is generous.

Baking one over sliced potatoes solves the other problem, which is that a whole fish gives up a lot of good liquid and it normally runs into a sheet pan and burns. Here it runs into starch instead. Rockfish, black bass, a small lingcod or a sea bream all work; what matters is that it fits your dish.

items: 2 lb (900 g) waxy potatoes, sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 whole rockfish, 2.5 to 3 lb (1.1 to 1.4 kg), scaled, gutted, gills out
1 lemon, half sliced and half in wedges

method: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss the potatoes, onion and garlic with the oil, salt, pepper and oregano and spread them in a baking dish just large enough to hold the fish on top.

Pour the wine over and bake the potatoes on their own until the edges are starting to colour and a knife goes into a slice with only slight resistance. They need this head start because the fish will be done long before raw potatoes would be.
Meanwhile prepare the fish. Check for scales the fishmonger missed by running a thumb from tail to head. Rinse the cavity, dry the fish inside and out, and slash both sides down to the bone twice.
Salt the fish inside and out, stuff the cavity with lemon slices and parsley, and rub the outside with oil.

Lay it on the potatoes, slide the dish back in, and bake until the skin has blistered and browned in patches and the flesh at the shoulder is opaque to the bone. A probe at the thickest point should read an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C).

The old test still works if you have no probe: push a thin knife into the thickest part behind the head and hold it there for five seconds, then touch it to your lip. Hot means done. Cool means keep going.
Rest the dish on the counter 5 minutes. Serve the fish straight from the dish, lifting the top fillet away from the backbone, then removing the whole skeleton before you work on the underside.
Squeeze lemon over and spoon the potatoes out from underneath, along with whatever has collected in the bottom of the dish. That liquid is the best thing on the table.

What goes wrong: an undercooked potato layer, because the fish went in at the same time. Give the base its head start and check that a slice from the middle of the dish is tender before the fish ever touches it.
notes: The cheeks, behind and slightly below the eye, are two coin-sized pieces of the best meat on the fish. Somebody in the kitchen should get them as payment.
A fish that will not fit the dish can have its head removed. It is not traditional and nobody at the table will care.
storage: Fridge, three days, fish picked off the bone and stored separately from the potatoes. The potatoes reheat well in a hot oven; the fish does not.

title: Dungeness Crab: Cooking, Cleaning and Picking
dek: Boil it hard, chill it fast, and do not let it sit in the pot congratulating itself.
intro:
A live Dungeness is about a quarter meat by weight, and every bit of the difference between a good one and a rubbery one happens in the twenty minutes after it goes in the pot. Crab overcooks the way an egg white overcooks, and the most common mistake is not the boiling time at all. It is leaving the crab in hot water after the burner goes off, which adds ten minutes of cooking nobody counted.

Big pot, hard boil, salted like the ocean, timed from the return to a boil, then straight into ice. Cleaning and picking follow, and both are less fiddly than they look once somebody shows you where the seam is.

items: 4 live Dungeness crab, about 2 lb (900 g) each
1/2 cup coarse salt, which is roughly seawater strength
1 large tub of ice water, about 8 quarts

method: Bring the salted water to a hard rolling boil in the largest pot you own. Crowding drops the temperature and everything after this depends on the water coming back up quickly.

Put the crab in head first, one at a time, and put the lid on. Some people clean the crab live before cooking, which is faster and arguably kinder; if you do that, the timing below drops by about a third and you are cooking halves rather than whole animals.

Start timing only when the water returns to a full boil. Figure roughly 15 minutes for a crab this size, adjusting for bigger or smaller ones. The shell turns from mottled purple-brown to a hard orange-red, and a leg pulled from the body comes away cleanly with the meat set inside it rather than jellied.
Lift them straight out and plunge them into the ice water. Do not leave crab in the cooling pot. Water at even a lazy simmer keeps cooking them, and rubbery crab is almost always crab that sat.
Chill until the shells are cold to the hand, about 10 minutes, then drain. Cold crab picks far more easily than warm crab because the meat firms and releases from the shell.
To clean: hold the crab with the legs toward you, get a thumb under the front lip of the top shell where it overhangs, and pull the carapace straight up and off. It comes away in one piece.

Flip the body and pull off the triangular apron on the underside. Scrape out the feathery grey gills from both sides with a thumb and rinse the cavity under cold water, taking the yellow crab butter with it or keeping it, depending on your household.
Break the body in half down the middle, then snap each half into leg sections. The meat sits in chambers along the body; crack them open with your thumbs and pick with a fork or the tip of a leg.

For the legs, crack each segment once with the back of a knife or a mallet, just enough to fracture the shell without shattering it into the meat. Push the meat out from the thick end with a thinner leg tip.
Serve with melted butter and lemon, or refrigerate the picked meat for cakes, a melt or a chowder.

What goes wrong, besides the pot: buying dead crab. A Dungeness that died before it was cooked breaks down fast and the meat goes mushy and bitter. Buy it live or buy it already cooked from someone who did it right.
notes: Crab seasons, size limits and sex restrictions on this coast are set by Fish and Wildlife and they change. Check with ODFW before you set a pot, not after.
Recreational crabbers should also check the current biotoxin closures published by the Oregon Department of Agriculture before eating anything they caught, including the viscera advisories.
storage: Whole cooked crab keeps two days in the fridge. Picked meat keeps three days and freezes badly, going stringy and watery, so pick it and use it.

title: Crab Cakes, Mostly Crab
dek: The binder should be embarrassed to be there.
intro:
Restaurant crab cakes are frequently a bread product with crab-adjacent notes, because crab is expensive and breadcrumbs are not. When you have picked the crab yourself, the calculation reverses entirely, and the job becomes holding large pieces of meat together with the smallest possible amount of anything else.

Two things make that possible. A long chill, which lets the egg and mayonnaise set up into something structural, and gentle folding that keeps the lumps of body meat intact. If you can see shreds instead of chunks, you have already lost.

items: 1 lb (450 g) picked Dungeness crab meat, drained and checked for shell
3 tbsp clarified butter or neutral oil

method: Spread the crab on a tray and go through it with your fingers under good light. Shell fragments in a crab cake ruin the whole idea, and they are exactly the colour of the meat.
Press the meat gently in a sieve to drain it. Wet crab needs more binder, and more binder is the thing you are trying to avoid.
Whisk the egg, mayonnaise, mustard, Worcestershire and lemon in a large bowl, then stir in panko, celery, chives, salt and cayenne. Let that sit two minutes so the crumbs hydrate.
Add the crab and fold with a rubber spatula, turning the bowl, no more than ten strokes. You are coating the meat, not mixing a batter.
Shape eight loose cakes about an inch thick, handling them like something fragile, which they are. Set them on a lined tray and refrigerate at least one hour and up to overnight.
Press the tops and bottoms into the remaining panko. Heat the butter in a heavy skillet over medium until a crumb sizzles steadily on contact.
Fry without crowding until the underside is a deep even brown and the cake feels set at the edges when you nudge it, then turn once with a wide spatula and a held breath.

They are ready when both faces are browned and the centre is hot through, reading an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) on a probe pushed in from the side. The crab is already cooked; you are heating and setting, not cooking it twice.
Drain on a rack and serve immediately with the tartare, stirred together, and a lemon wedge.

What goes wrong: flipping a cake that has not set. If the spatula meets resistance, wait. And do not press the cakes flat in the pan, which squeezes out the moisture that is holding the whole thing together.
notes: Body meat and leg meat behave differently. Body meat is the flaky stuff that binds; leg meat is the chunks you want to see. Use both.
If the mix is too loose to shape after chilling, add panko one tablespoon at a time. Adding egg makes it wetter, not firmer, which surprises people.
storage: Raw shaped cakes keep a day in the fridge and freeze well on a tray before bagging. Cooked cakes keep two days and reheat acceptably in a hot oven on a rack.

title: The Crab Melt
dek: An open-faced sandwich that has no business being as good as it is.
intro:
This is what happens to the crab that did not get eaten standing over the sink. It is a counter lunch, not a dinner party, and it is quietly one of the best uses of Dungeness there is, because the cheese and the toast take a small amount of crab a very long way.

The only real technique is keeping it under the broiler rather than in the oven. You want the top browned and bubbling before the bread underneath has time to go soft, which is a matter of about four minutes of close attention and one open oven door.

items: 12 oz (340 g) picked crab meat, drained
4 thick slices sourdough or a split ciabatta

method: Set an oven rack about six inches under the broiler element and turn the broiler on to preheat. A cold broiler browns nothing and just dries the sandwich out.
Fold the crab mix ingredients together lightly, keeping the lumps whole. Taste it. It should be a shade under-seasoned, because the cheese is bringing salt.

Butter the bread on both sides and toast it in a dry skillet over medium until the underside is golden and crisp and the slice sounds hollow when tapped. Rub the toasted face once with the cut garlic.
Lay the toast on a sheet pan, toasted face up. Add tomato slices if you are using them, then pile the crab mix on and spread it to the edges. Bare bread at the edge burns before the middle heats.
Cover generously with both cheeses, all the way to the crust.

Broil, with the door open and your eyes on it, until the cheese has melted, pooled and browned in blisters across the top and the crab underneath is steaming. It goes from pale to perfect to ruined in under a minute at the end.

If you want to be sure the middle is hot, slide a probe in from the side; an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C) means it is heated through, which matters more if the crab came out of the fridge cold.
Let it settle a minute before cutting, or the whole topping slides off in one piece and lands on the board.
What goes wrong: too much mayonnaise. It loosens under heat and runs out from under the cheese, and you end up with a soggy raft. Keep the mix stiff.
notes: Shrimp works, canned salmon works, hot-smoked salmon works if you cut it with something plain. This is a template.
Sourdough holds up under a wet topping far better than a soft sandwich loaf, which turns to pulp.
storage: Assembled melts do not keep. The crab mix keeps two days in the fridge and is also a fine thing to eat with crackers while deciding whether to bother with the toast.

title: Steamed Clams in Butter and Wine
dek: Ten minutes, one pan, and the broth is the point.
yield: Serves 4 as a starter, 2 as dinner
intro:
Steamed clams are a fifteen minute dinner with one hour of waiting in front of them, and the waiting is not optional. Clams from a bay or a beach carry sand, and a bowl of gritty clams is a bowl nobody finishes. An hour in cold salted water gives them time to pump the sand out on their own.

After that it is a hot pan, some aromatics, a splash of wine, a lid, and enough restraint to pull the clams out as they open rather than waiting for the last stubborn one. The broth left behind is better than the clams and there should be bread ready for it.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) manila or littleneck clams
3 tbsp salt for the purge water
3 tbsp cold butter, cubed, for finishing
1 loaf crusty bread, thickly sliced and toasted

method: Dissolve the salt in the cold water and let the clams sit in it, in a bowl in the fridge, for an hour. Do not use fresh water alone; it kills them and they stop purging. Lift the clams out of the water rather than pouring, so the sand stays at the bottom.
Scrub the shells and sort them. Any clam with a cracked shell goes in the bin. Any clam gaping open should close when you tap it firmly; if it does not, it is dead and it goes too.

Heat the butter and oil in a wide pan with a lid over medium. Cook the garlic, shallot and chile until the garlic is fragrant and just turning pale gold at the edges, which takes about a minute and turns bitter in two.
Pour in the wine, raise the heat, and let it bubble hard for a minute so the raw alcohol cooks off and the flavour concentrates.

Add the clams, put the lid on, and shake the pan once. Steam over high heat, lifting the lid every minute or so, and remove clams to a bowl with tongs as they gape wide open. They do not open at the same rate and the early ones turn to erasers waiting for the late ones.
When the great majority have opened, take the pan off the heat. Discard any clam that stayed shut after everything else opened.

Let the broth settle for a moment, then pour it off carefully, leaving the last spoonful with any grit behind. Return it to the pan, bring it to a simmer, and swirl in the cold butter a cube at a time until the broth turns glossy and slightly thickened.
Return the clams, add parsley and a squeeze of lemon, and serve straight from the pan with toast for the broth.
What goes wrong: overcooking. A clam that has been in the pan two minutes past opening is chewy and tastes of nothing. Pull them as they go.
notes: Anyone harvesting their own should check the current shellfish biotoxin closures published by the Oregon Department of Agriculture before digging. Closures for domoic acid and paralytic shellfish poisoning are not visible in the clam and not affected by cooking.
A licence is required to harvest shellfish in this state, and the rules are ODFW's. Look them up rather than guessing.
storage: Live clams keep a day or two in the fridge in an open bowl under a damp towel, never sealed in a bag and never in water. Cooked clams keep a day and are best picked out of the shell and dropped into a chowder.

title: Razor Clams, Cleaned and Fried
dek: Two minutes in the pan, and the cleaning is the whole job.
intro:
A razor clam is the reason people stand on a cold beach at night with a flashlight and a tube. It does not taste like a steamer clam and it does not cook like one. The meat is tender, sweet and almost creamy, and it goes from that to a piece of belt leather in roughly ninety seconds of unnecessary heat.

The cleaning is the part that puts people off, and it is genuinely a bit of work the first few times. After that it takes about a minute a clam. The frying is barely a recipe: hot fat, a light crumb, one turn, out.

items: 8 cups boiling water for the dip
1.5 cups fine cracker crumbs or panko

method: Dip the clams, a few at a time, into boiling water for five to ten seconds, just until the shells crack apart, then straight into ice water. Any longer and you have begun cooking them, which you will regret at the pan.
Slide the shells off and the clam out. Cut off the tip of the neck and the dark tip of the digger foot.
Snip the clam open lengthwise from the neck through the body so it opens flat like a book. Cut away the gills, the dark gut running along the body, and the tough zipper-like piece near the base.

Rinse each cleaned clam under cold running water, rubbing the surface with your thumbs to get every trace of sand from the folds. Sand is the entire reason a fried razor clam ever disappoints anybody.
Dry the cleaned clams hard between towels. Wet clams will not hold a crumb and will spit in the fat.
Set up three shallow dishes: flour with the salt, pepper and cayenne; eggs beaten with the milk; crumbs. Coat each clam flour, egg, crumb, pressing the crumbs on, and lay them on a rack.

Heat the butter and oil in a wide skillet over medium-high until the butter foam has subsided and a dropped crumb browns within a few seconds. This has to be hot; a cool pan means a longer cook and a tough clam.

Fry in batches, no crowding, until the underside is golden and the edges of the clam have just started to curl, roughly a minute, then turn once and give the second side about the same. Cooked razor clam is opaque white and still yielding; if it has shrunk noticeably and gone rigid, it is past.

If you want the number, seafood is fully cooked at an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C), but a razor clam is thin enough that it arrives there almost immediately. Time and appearance are the practical guide here.
Drain on a rack, salt lightly, and serve with lemon and nothing else that needs cooking.
notes: Razor clam beaches close for domoic acid, sometimes for long stretches. Check the current closures with the Oregon Department of Agriculture before you dig, every single time. Cooking does not destroy the toxin and there is no way to see it.

Digging requires a licence and there are daily limits, including the rule that you keep the first clams you dig regardless of size. That is ODFW's rule, not ours, and it is worth reading before you go.
storage: Cleaned raw clams keep a day in the fridge and freeze well, laid flat in a bag with the air pressed out, for three months. Fried clams keep for about as long as it takes to carry the plate to the table.

title: Chowder Built on Shells
dek: The bones and shells you were about to throw out are the ingredient.
intro:
Every crab you pick and every fish you fillet leaves behind the part that has the most flavour in it. Shells, heads and frames are where the gelatin and the sweetness live, and forty minutes of gentle simmering pulls it all into water for nothing. A chowder built on that base tastes like the ocean; the same chowder built on bought stock tastes like a soup with fish in it.

Two rules. Do not simmer fish bones for hours, because they turn bitter and glue-like after about forty minutes. And roast crab shells first, because raw shell stock tastes flat and roasted shell stock tastes like a bisque.

items: 4 crab bodies and shells, or 2 fish frames and heads, gills removed
4 oz (110 g) salt pork or bacon, diced
2 lb (900 g) waxy potatoes, in 3/4 inch dice
1 tsp fine sea salt, plus more to taste
1 lb (450 g) picked crab, clams or flaked cooked fish

method: For crab shells, heat the oven to 400°F (205°C), toss the shells with the oil, and roast until they have darkened to a deep red-orange and smell sweet and toasty rather than raw. Fish frames skip this step; they are better unroasted.
Put the shells or frames in a stockpot with the vegetables, wine, cold water and aromatics. Start from cold water, which draws more out than dropping bones into hot water does.
Bring it slowly up until the surface just trembles, skimming the grey foam off as it rises. Never let it boil. A boiling stock emulsifies fat and scum back into itself and comes out cloudy and muddy.

Simmer crab shells 45 minutes and fish frames no more than 30. Fish bones give up everything they have in half an hour and turn bitter shortly after. Strain through a fine sieve and press gently; do not force it.
Render the salt pork in a heavy pot over medium heat until the fat runs and the pieces are golden and crisp at the edges. Lift them out and reserve.
Add the butter, onion and celery and cook until soft and translucent with no colour, then stir in the flour and cook it until the raw smell is gone and it coats everything in a pale paste.

Whisk in 8 cups of the shell stock a little at a time, then add the potatoes, thyme, salt and pepper. Simmer until the potatoes surrender completely to a knife tip and the broth has thickened enough to coat the back of a spoon.
Crush a few potato cubes against the side of the pot to release their starch, which thickens more cleanly than adding flour a second time.

Stir in the cream and bring it back to steaming, then take it off the heat before adding the seafood. Picked crab and cooked fish need warming, not cooking; give them 3 minutes off the burner under a lid, and check that anything raw reaches an internal temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit (63°C).
Finish with parsley, lemon juice and the reserved salt pork. Taste for salt at the very end, since the stock, the pork and the shellfish have all been seasoning it behind your back.
notes: Freeze shells and frames as you generate them, in a bag in the freezer, until there is enough for a pot. They keep three months without much loss.
Gills must come out of a fish head before it goes in the pot. They hold blood and grit and they are the main reason people think fish stock tastes muddy.
storage: Strained stock keeps four days in the fridge and six months frozen. Finished chowder keeps two days and does not freeze once the cream and seafood are in.
